summary: Specifies how the Shim6 protocol detects failures between two communicating nodes, and an exploration protocol that switches to another pair of addresses if a failure occurs and a working pair can be found.

eli5.summary: When a road is blocked, you try another one. This note describes how two computers notice a blockage and test other address pairs until one works.

questions: what is the reach protocol for ipv6 multihoming
what are the shim6 keepalive and probe messages
subtitle: How two IPv6 hosts notice a dead path and quietly switch to another pair of addresses.

tldr.problem: A multihomed IPv6 host has several addresses, and a failure on the path between one pair of addresses should not break an ongoing conversation.
tldr.mechanism: REAP watches payload traffic in both directions, sends Keepalive messages only when traffic flows one way, and when replies stop it sends Probe messages over different address pairs until both sides agree on a working one.
tldr.outcome: It is the failure detection and locator pair exploration part of Shim6, a Proposed Standard from June 2009. It is deliberately lightweight and conservative, and it cannot match mechanisms that know about applications.

today: RFC 5534 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the failure detection part of Shim6, which is defined in RFC 5533.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5533 defines Shim6, an IP-layer mechanism that extends IPv6 to support multihoming and hides it from applications. This RFC specifies one part of it: detecting that the pair of addresses (or interfaces) in use between two nodes has failed, and picking another pair. The RFC calls these failure detection and locator pair exploration, and the combined protocol is the REAchability Protocol (REAP).

Failure detection is made as lightweight as possible. Idle communication generates no packets, and traffic flowing in both directions needs no extra packets either. Only when traffic goes one way does a node send keepalives in the other direction. If there is outgoing traffic but no incoming traffic or keepalives, there must be a failure, and exploration starts.

REAP treats an address as synonymous with a locator. Other parts of Shim6 make sure the locators of a node belong together; REAP does not.
sections.eli5: If you keep talking and the other side keeps answering, nobody worries. Only when the answers stop do you start looking for another way to reach them.

sections.title: Addresses, Pairs and Their States
sections.content:
The RFC defines two levels of failure detection. An address is available when it is assigned to an interface, its prefix lifetime has not expired, it is not tentative, it is a global unicast or unique local address, and local policy accepts it. It is locally operational when the interface is up, a suitable default router is known to be reachable, and nothing local says the address is unusable. Implementations MUST be able to use Neighbor Unreachability Detection for this.

The second level is the address pair. A bidirectionally operational pair carries packets in both directions. A unidirectionally operational pair works in one direction only, which can happen because of ingress filtering or network failures. Shim6 implementations MUST support discovering operational pairs through explicit reachability tests and Forced Bidirectional Detection.

The primary address pair is what upper-layer protocols see. The current address pair is the single pair used until problems occur, because Shim6 does not send one transport connection over several paths at once.
sections.eli5: Having a phone number that rings is not the same as being able to talk. A pair of addresses only counts as working when messages really get through.

sections.title: Detecting Failure with Forced Bidirectional Detection
sections.content:
Failure detection tracks local information, tracks what the peer reports, and verifies reachability. For verification, REAP uses Forced Bidirectional Detection (FBD): whenever payload goes out in one direction, something should come back. That can be data, transport acknowledgments or a REAP Keepalive.

Each context has two mutually exclusive timers. When a node sends a payload packet, it starts a timer for the return traffic, set to Send Timeout. When it receives one, it stops that timer and starts a timer for its own response, set to Keepalive Timeout. If no packet has gone out within the Keepalive Interval, a Keepalive is sent. The RECOMMENDED interval is one-half to one-third of the Keepalive Timeout, and the actual values SHOULD be randomized to prevent synchronization.

If Send Timeout seconds pass after a payload packet with no return traffic, full reachability exploration starts. A node that uses a non-default Send Timeout tells its peer through the Keepalive Timeout option.
sections.eli5: If you talk and get no answer, someone might be gone. So whoever is only listening says 'still here' now and then, and if even that stops, you know something broke.

sections.title: Exploring Address Pairs
sections.content:
With nA and nB addresses on the two sides, there are nA * nB pairs, and the RFC counts twice that many two-way combinations, so full exploration is expensive. REAP only does it when a failure is suspected. The node that first notices the problem sends Probe messages over different address pairs in turn. A peer that receives a Probe reporting a problem starts its own parallel exploration in the other direction, because pairs may work in one direction only.

The candidate list comes from combining the node's addresses with the peer's addresses, pruned and ordered by the RFC 3484 default address selection rules and by local preferences. Nodes SHOULD try all candidates until a working pair is found, but MUST do so sequentially and with exponential back-off, to avoid a signaling storm.

The Initial Probe Timeout is 0.5 seconds and the Number of Initial Probes is 4, sent at a fixed rate before back-off begins. The Max Probe Timeout is 60 seconds, which is the limit for the probe interval. Exploration is run only for an already established session, because using it during connection establishment would create an amplification vulnerability.
sections.eli5: When the usual road is closed, you try the other roads one at a time, waiting a bit longer after each try so you do not cause a traffic jam. Both of you search, because a road may work for one direction only.

sections.title: Keepalive and Probe Messages
sections.content:
REAP adds two Shim6 control messages. The Keepalive message has Type 66, carries a Receiver Context Tag (a 47-bit field), and has no useful options defined. The Probe message has Type 67 and carries counts of sent and received probes (Psent and Precvd, each 4 bits), a 2-bit Sta state field, and for each probe a source address, a destination address, a 32-bit Probe Nonce and 32-bit Probe Data.

The Probe Nonce lets the sender match a received probe to a sent one, so it is highly RECOMMENDED to make it hard to guess, using a good random number generator as outlined in RFC 4086. Probe Data has no fixed meaning and is copied back unchanged. A Probe also echoes recently received probes, which is how each side learns which of its probes arrived.

The Keepalive Timeout option (Type 10, Length 4) carries a 16-bit Keepalive Timeout value in seconds and may be sent in the I2, I2bis, R2 or UPDATE messages.
sections.eli5: A Keepalive is a quick 'still here'. A Probe is a note with a secret number that says 'I tried this route and here is what I heard back'.

sections.title: The Three-State Behavior
sections.content:
On each context a node is in one of three states. In Operational the address pairs are assumed to work. In Exploring the node has seen no traffic from the peer for more than a Send Timer period. In InboundOK the node sees traffic from the peer, but the peer may not yet see traffic from it. The Send Timer runs in Operational and InboundOK, the Keepalive Timer only in Operational, and no timer runs in Exploring.

A Send Timeout moves a node to Exploring and sends a Probe with State 1. Receiving a payload packet, Keepalive or Probe in Exploring moves it to InboundOK. Receiving a Probe with State InboundOk moves it to Operational and chooses a new current address pair from the reports of received probes. Receiving a Probe with State Operational ends exploration. Until a new pair is confirmed, payload packets keep going to the previously used addresses.
sections.eli5: Each side is either 'all is well', 'I hear nothing' or 'I hear you but I am not sure you hear me'. They keep trading notes until both say all is well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attackers may spoof ICMP errors or router and address information to make the peers believe addresses are or are not operational. REAP provides no protection for those indications, so they SHOULD NOT be taken as proof of connectivity problems. REAP does run its own tests before picking a new pair, which gives weak resistance, but denial of service and on-path attackers remain a problem.

An on-path attacker who sees a context tag can send spoofed Keepalives once per Send Timeout interval to stop two nodes from sending their own, which is relevant only to one-way communication and makes the nodes explore needlessly. Off-path attackers face 47-bit random context tags. Because IPsec operates above Shim6, it cannot protect exploration against on-path attackers.

Exploration can also amplify flooding, which is why Shim6 does not support REAP during connection establishment. The Probe Nonces act as a return routability check against third-party flooding.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could shout fake 'still here' messages. Secret numbers in the messages make it hard for outsiders to fake them, but someone standing right in the middle of the path can still cause trouble.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
With no failures, the cost is small: no keepalives are sent when a context is idle or when traffic flows in both directions, so a session moving from active to idle produces only one or two keepalives. After a failure, one keepalive and then a series of probes are sent per active context, and all of them time out within 15 seconds. The RFC puts peak traffic at around one packet per second per context.

The exponential back-off reduces probing until it reaches one packet per context per minute. Shim6 uses the same header for signaling and for payload after a rehoming event, so fate is shared between them. One exception is a path MTU discovery black hole, where payload fails but signaling works; if only large packets are sent, exploration will likely select another path.
sections.eli5: When all is quiet, nobody says anything. After a break, there is a short burst of messages that quickly slows down, so the network is not flooded.

viz.caption: REAP STATES AND SOME KEY TRANSITIONS
VALUES OF THE PROBE STATE FIELD

items.label: Operational
items.desc: Sender believes there is no problem in either direction.

items.label: Exploring
items.desc: Sender has a problem, for example no traffic seen from the recipient.

items.label: InboundOk
items.desc: Sender sees packets from the recipient, but the recipient has a problem or has not confirmed it is resolved.
